newsitem.title: USA: Nissan to cut jobs, sees flat sales in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Nissan to cut jobs, sees flat sales in 1997.

text.p: Saying it needs to update its sales and marketing organization, Nissan Motor Corp. U.S.A. said Tuesday it was offering early retirement and voluntary separation programs in order to cut 450 employees and expected additional layoffs.

Bob Thomas, chief executive officer of Nissan Motor Corp. U.S.A., said the firm was making its offer to about 2,000 of its 2,500 sales and marketing workers in the United States. However, there are about 250 people eligible for the retirement program, and there is a 200-person limit on the separation deal.
The company, based in Torrance, Calif., is the sales and markeing arm of Japanese automaker Nissan Motor Co. Ltd. Thomas made the announcement at the North American International Auto Show here.
Nissan employs a total of more than 20,000 people in North America.

Thomas refused to put a figure on the total number of job reductions Nissan expected, saying the company itself has not determined the number. He also declined to identify what parts of the operation were being eliminated.
Nissan, which has not restructured in its approximately 30 years in the U.S. market, is taking the action to respond to marketplace changes such as the rise of auto superstore dealers, Thomas said.
The changes are also being driven by a desire to be more entrepreneurial and customer-focused, he said. The layoffs were not forced on the unit by its Japanese parent, Thomas said.
"We're profitable, we're successful. We see the world changing," he said, adding Nissan's U.S. product development and manufacturing operations are not being affected by the layoffs.

Nissan, including its Infiniti luxury division, expects flat annual sales in the 750,000 range for 1997 and 1998, he said. The company has a goal of 900,000 units by 2000. It reported about 750,000 in sales for 1996, a decline of about 3 percent from 1994.

The company plans to introduce a new version of its Altima sedan in June, with annual sales seen at 170,000, up from 150,000 for all of 1996. The car was introduced at the Detroit show by a live version of Nissan's popular "Toys" commercial in which an action figure steals a woman from her boyfriend.
Four months after the Altima, Nissan will introduce its redesigned pickup truck. Industry analysts have said the automaker is also working on a new sport utility vehilce for the U.S. market.
